prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Apply famous investors' frameworks to the publicly listed company "DEERE & CO" (ticker DE). Use the most recent information you know. Be specific (names, numbers, years). Never invent figures.
Reply with ONLY one JSON object:
{"summaries": { "<framework id>": "2-3 plain sentences on how well the company fits this investor's approach, written neutrally" } for EVERY framework below:
   "gardner": David Gardner: Rule Breaker Investing (The six Rule Breaker traits (Motley Fool Rule Breakers; “Rule Breakers, Rule Makers”, 1998))
   "buffett": Warren Buffett (Berkshire Hathaway shareholder letters; tenets summarised in “The Warren Buffett Way” (Hagstrom))
   "munger": Charlie Munger (Munger's talks and “Poor Charlie's Almanack”)
   "lynch": Peter Lynch (“One Up on Wall Street” and “Beating the Street”)

   "gerstner": Brad Gerstner (His public letters (e.g. “Time to Get Fit”, 2022) and interviews (BG2 podcast); a summary, not an official checklist)
   "druckenmiller": Stanley Druckenmiller (His public interviews and speeches; a summary, not an official checklist)
   "smith": Terry Smith (Fundsmith owner's manual and annual letters (“buy good companies, don't overpay, do nothing”))

   "pabrai": Mohnish Pabrai (“The Dhandho Investor”)

   "valentine": Don Valentine (His talks (e.g. Stanford GSB, 2010) on what Sequoia looks for)
   "nash": Tom Nash: the 12-step research process (“How to Find the Best Stocks in the Market” (Tom Nash, 2026))
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence"} } for EVERY id below (each question is shared by the frameworks that ask it):
   "momentum": Has the share price risen strongly over roughly the last six to twelve months, beating the market?
   "g4": Is it run by great leaders and backed by smart, well-known investors or partners?
   "g6": Do commentators and analysts commonly call the stock overvalued (a trait Gardner sees as a good sign)?
   "simple": Is it an established business simple enough for a careful generalist to understand well?
   "b2": Has it shown consistent results over many years?
   "integrity": Is management honest and candid with shareholders, rational with capital, paid in a way that lines up with owners, and well governed?
   "b6": Does management avoid copying peers or empire-building for its own sake?
   "roic": Does it earn a high, consistent return on the capital it uses, without relying on debt?
   "fcf": Does it turn most of its profit into plenty of free cash flow?
   "b10": Has the money it kept (instead of paying out) grown the company's value by at least as much?
   "safety": Is the share price well below a conservative estimate of the business's value (a margin of safety)?
   "fairprice": Is the price reasonable for the quality and growth on offer?
   "mu5": Thinking backwards, are there few ways this business could fail?
   "reinvest": Can it reinvest its profits at high returns for many years?
   "ly2": Does it fit a clear category (fast grower, stalwart, turnaround…) with a simple story for its future?
   "ly3": Is the price/earnings ratio at or below the earnings growth rate?
   "runway": Can its sales keep growing substantially for many years, into new places or products?
   "ly7": Are insiders buying and is the company reducing its share count?
   "ly8": Is it overlooked by Wall Street or in a 'boring' niche?
   "fi2": Is management committed to developing new products as current ones mature?
   "fi3": Does its R&D spending produce results?
   "fi4": Is it unusually good at selling?
   "longterm": Does management put long-term value and innovation ahead of short-term profit?
   "gr1": Is it a large, established company?
   "ni10": Has it been profitable in each of the last ten years?
   "gr4": Has it paid a dividend every year for at least 20 years?
   "eps10": Has earnings per share grown by at least one third over ten years?
   "gr6": Is the share price no more than about 15 times average earnings?
   "gr7": Is price/earnings × price/book no more than about 22.5?
   "th1": Does it have proprietary technology about ten times better than the next best?
   "timing": Is the technology and market timing right for this business now?
   "th3": Did it start with a big share of a small market, and can it expand from there?
   "team": Is it led by an exceptional founder or world-class management team?
   "th5": Does it have a way to reach and sell to customers, not just a product?
   "durable": Will its market position still hold in 10 to 20 years, resisting disruption and obsolescence?
   "th7": Has it found a unique opportunity that others don't see?
   "trend": Is it a leading beneficiary of a major platform shift or secular trend (such as AI or cloud computing)?
   "dr1": Are earnings accelerating and analysts' estimates moving up?
   "dr2": Will the business look better in 18–24 months than today, beyond what is already obvious?
   "dr4": Do interest rates, central-bank liquidity and the economy work in its favour?
   "dr6": Are there identifiable events that could drive results higher?
   "dr7": Is conviction high enough that it could be a large, concentrated position?
   "gm": Is the gross margin high, a sign of pricing power?
   "fcfyield": Is the free-cash-flow yield reasonable or attractive for its quality and growth?
   "gb2": Is operating profit high compared with the whole company's value (enterprise value)?
   "pa2": Is the business or industry going through a temporary, fixable setback?
   "pa4": Is the chance of permanent loss small even if the outcome is uncertain?
   "wo1": Is it a leader in AI, robotics, energy storage, blockchain or multiomic sequencing?
   "wo2": Are its product costs falling quickly as volumes grow, opening up big new demand?
   "wo3": Does it combine several innovation platforms?
   "wo4": Could its addressable market be many times larger in five years?
   "ac3": Is it largely insulated from commodity prices, interest rates and similar outside forces?
   "ns1": Does it pass the savings from its growing size back to customers, making it ever harder to compete with?
   "ns4": Is its likely position in 10–20 years clearly stronger than today?
   "va2": Does the product solve a large, painful problem?
   "tn1": Does it sell into a real secular trend (like AI, energy or robotics; ideally the infrastructure layer), as a company built for that trend rather than an old business retrofitting?
   "tn2": Is there a gap between the story the market tells about the company and what it is actually becoming (like Palantir seen as a consultancy, Tesla as a car company)?
   "tn3": Is it outside the zones to avoid: small caps, Chinese companies, commodity producers, airlines, seasonal businesses and startups?
   "tn4": Of these three, does it pass at least two (and have a valid reason for any miss, such as infrastructure needing leverage or a clear path to profit): revenue grown for the past few years, profitable, more cash than debt?
   "tn5": Has free cash flow been positive, and cash exceeded debt, in each of the last 4 to 6 quarters?
   "tn6": Is revenue growing at 10% a year or more?
   "tn7": Is revenue growth % plus free-cash-flow margin % at least 40?
   "tn8": Over the last year, did revenue grow faster than total operating expenses?
   "tn9": Does it avoid every instant kill: market cap under $1B, more debt than cash, short interest above 10%, operating margin below 20%, revenue growth below 10% and falling, two or more earnings misses in the last 4 quarters, or less than 10 years since founding?
   "tn10": Is it free of any major regulatory or legal threat?
   "tn11": Can it be stated plainly as “provides X that helps Y achieve Z, and charges [revenue model]”, with a clear answer to what pain it cures, who is in pain, and why customers choose it over competitors?
   "tn13": Score it on Nash's 13 categories, 0, 5 or 10 each, using the last twelve months: cash vs debt (more debt / more cash / 2x+ cash), revenue growth (<10% / 10-20% / >20%), operating margin (<10% / 10-25% / >25%), short interest (>10% / 5-10% / <5%), institutional ownership (<30% / 30-60% / >60%), revenue growing faster than expenses (no 0 / yes 10), 5-year return vs the S&P 500 (behind / ahead by 10-20% / ahead by 20%+), and, judged harshly, moat, CEO, recession-proof pricing power, secular trend, culture and mission, talent (none / some / strong). Is the total 75 or more? Give the total in the evidence.
   "tn14": Over the last five years, has revenue grown every year, operating margin expanded, free cash flow been positive and rising, and cash exceeded debt every year?
   "tn15": Would a banker lend to it: interest coverage (operating income ÷ interest) of 4x or more, assets (excluding goodwill) at least 2× liabilities, current ratio of 1 or more, and total liabilities under 4× equity?
   "tn18": Does the CEO have a track record of execution (growth, margins, innovation), skin in the game through open-market share purchases, and 10+ years in the role, ideally as founder?
   "tn20": Has it consistently beaten earnings expectations?
   "tn21": Is it free of every red flag: a clown CEO, a co-CEO structure, an acquisition spree, any suspicion of fraud or accounting problems, an auditor change, declining margins, revenue spiking while inventory piles up, or insiders selling hard while the stock runs?
   "tn22": Does it avoid the hype trap of no revenue, weak fundamentals, constant share sales to raise cash and nonstop media hype?
   "tn24": Working back from today's price, is the growth the price implies below what the company is already delivering?
   "tn25": With Nash's DCF (3-year averages of revenue growth and FCF margin, trimmed growth, 5 years of free cash flow, 4% terminal growth, plus cash minus debt), is the value per share above today's price even at a 12% discount rate?
   "tn26": Using the multiple that fits (forward P/E vs peers for mature companies, hardware and banks; Rule of 40 for software; price to sales vs the industry for unprofitable growth), is it attractive, with a PEG (forward P/E ÷ EPS growth) of 1 or less?

summaries.gardner: Deere is a top dog in farm equipment with a strong brand and a lead in precision-ag and autonomy, and its shares rose about 39% from October 2025 to October 2026, but it is a 189-year-old cyclical industrial rather than a leader of a young, fast-emerging industry. It fits only some Rule Breaker traits.
summaries.buffett: Deere has a durable brand and dealer moat, an understandable business, rising dividends and a shrinking share count (diluted shares fell from 316.6M in FY2020 to 270.7M in Q3 FY2026), but earnings swing widely with the farm cycle and the stock trades near 36 times trailing earnings, leaving little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Deere is the kind of high-quality franchise Munger admired, with a decades-long lead in large farm machinery and growing tech lock-in, and few plausible ways to fail outright. The main issues are cyclicality, a captive finance arm that adds leverage, and a full price.
summaries.lynch: Deere is a cyclical in Lynch's terms, best bought when earnings are depressed and the P/E looks high; FY2025 EPS fell to $18.50 from $34.63 in FY2023, and the trailing P/E of about 36 is far above its growth rate. It is well understood and widely followed rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: Deere scores well on Fisher's points for R&D ($2.31B in FY2025), a powerful dealer sales organization, long-term product development (See & Spray, autonomy) and conservative management. Its margins are cyclical rather than steadily rising.
summaries.graham: Deere passes Graham's size, ten-year profit, long dividend record and ten-year EPS growth tests (EPS $5.77 in FY2015 to $18.50 in FY2025), but fails on price: about 24 times three-year average earnings and P/E times P/B above 200.
summaries.thiel: Deere is a durable incumbent with a strong distribution channel and growing proprietary technology, but it is not a monopoly built on technology ten times better than rivals, and it did not start by dominating a small new market.
summaries.gerstner: Deere is a disciplined, profitable company with clear 2030 targets (10% sales CAGR, 20% mid-cycle operating margin), but its growth is cyclical rather than secular and its valuation already prices a recovery; it is not an obvious AI beneficiary outside construction demand from data centers.
summaries.druckenmiller: The setup turned positive in 2026 as Deere raised its FY2026 net income outlook to $4.75-5.00B, construction demand rose with data-center and infrastructure work, and the stock outperformed; the risks are a still-falling large-ag cycle, about $1B a year of tariff costs into FY2027 and interest-rate sensitivity.
summaries.smith: Deere is a good company with pricing power and a strong brand, but Terry Smith's high and steady returns on capital without leverage are not met: earnings are cyclical, gross margins near 28% are modest, and the finance arm carries most of $63.8B of debt; at about 36 times earnings it is not cheap.
summaries.greenblatt: On the Magic Formula Deere scores poorly at today's price: operating profit of $6.0B against an enterprise value of roughly $227B is an earnings yield under 3%, even though equipment returns on capital are good mid-cycle.
summaries.akre: Deere has a strong business and capable, shareholder-minded management, and it reinvests in technology and buybacks, but its ability to compound reinvested capital at high rates is limited by the farm cycle.
summaries.pabrai: Deere's farm downturn is a temporary, fixable setback and permanent loss risk is low, but the shares already trade at a premium multiple, so it lacks the heads-I-win low-price setup Pabrai looks for.
summaries.wood: Deere is a credible leader in agricultural robotics and computer vision (See & Spray, autonomous tractors), but it remains a hardware-led industrial whose costs are not falling on an exponential curve; it is a partial fit with ARK's robotics theme.
summaries.ackman: Deere fits several of Ackman's criteria: simple, predictable over a cycle, dominant, with high barriers to entry, but it is exposed to commodity prices, interest rates and tariffs, and its finance arm makes the balance sheet more leveraged than he prefers.
summaries.sleep: Deere shares some scale benefits with customers through technology that cuts input costs, such as reported herbicide savings of over 50% from See & Spray, but it mostly captures scale gains as margin rather than passing them on, so it is not a classic scale-economics-shared business.
summaries.valentine: Deere solves a large, important problem, feeding the world with less labor and fewer inputs, but it is a mature incumbent rather than the early-stage, huge-market venture Valentine sought.
summaries.nash: Deere fails several of Nash's screens: revenue is falling or growing well under 10%, debt far exceeds cash because of John Deere Financial, operating margin is about 13% and the stock trades near 36 times earnings. It scores well on moat, durability and being outside the zones to avoid.

momentum.evidence: The share price rose from about $462 at the end of October 2025 to $641.63 on October 16, 2026, roughly 39%, well ahead of the broad market.

g4.evidence: CEO John May has a solid record and Deere partners with firms such as SpaceX's Starlink for connectivity, but it has no famous founder or celebrity investor backing.

g6.evidence: At about 36 times trailing earnings in a farm downturn, many commentators call Deere fully or over-valued, though consensus still leans positive.

simple.evidence: Deere builds and finances tractors, combines, mowers and construction machines sold through dealers, an easy business to understand.

b2.evidence: Deere has been profitable for decades, but net income swung from $2.75B in FY2020 to $10.17B in FY2023 and back to $5.03B in FY2025.

integrity.evidence: Management gives clear segment guidance, returns cash through dividends ($1.72B in FY2025) and buybacks, and ties pay to shareholder value added; no accounting controversies are known.

b6.evidence: Deere has made focused tech acquisitions such as Blue River Technology ($305M, 2017) and Bear Flag Robotics (2021) rather than empire-building deals.

roic.evidence: Return on equity was about 21% in FY2025, but that relies on a leveraged captive finance arm; equipment operations earn high returns mid-cycle and Deere targets 45% operating return on assets.

fcf.evidence: FY2025 operating cash flow of $7.459B minus capex of $1.36B left about $6.1B of free cash flow, more than net income of $5.03B.

b10.evidence: Since FY2015 EPS rose from $5.77 to $18.50 in FY2025 while diluted shares fell, showing retained earnings created more value than they cost.

safety.evidence: At $641.63 the stock trades at about 36 times trailing EPS of $17.99 and over 6 times book value, with no margin of safety on conservative estimates.

fairprice.evidence: The price is high on trough earnings but more reasonable against mid-cycle EPS, which was $25.62 in FY2024 and $34.63 at the FY2023 peak.

mu5.evidence: With a dominant brand, dealer network and installed base in an essential industry, Deere has few plausible paths to outright failure; the main risks are cycles and credit losses.

reinvest.evidence: Deere reinvests about $2.3B a year in R&D with good returns on tech like See & Spray, but core markets grow slowly so much of the cash goes to buybacks and dividends.

ly2.evidence: It is a classic cyclical: earnings fall in farm downturns and recover with crop prices and fleet replacement.

ly3.evidence: The trailing P/E of about 36 is far above recent earnings growth, which has been negative since FY2023.

runway.evidence: Deere targets a 10% net sales CAGR to 2030 from precision tech, construction and aftermarket, but core farm machinery is a mature, cyclical market.

ly7.evidence: Deere cut diluted shares from 316.6M in FY2020 to 270.7M in Q3 FY2026, but there is no evidence of notable insider open-market buying.

ly8.evidence: Deere is a widely followed large-cap covered by about 25 analysts.

fi2.evidence: Deere keeps developing new products such as See & Spray, autonomous tillage tractors and SmartGrade construction tech as older lines mature.

fi3.evidence: R&D of $2.311B in FY2025 produced products customers buy: about one-third of North American sprayers on order carry See & Spray, and factory SmartGrade adoption rose over 50% in FY2026 year to date.

fi4.evidence: Deere's dealer network and in-house financing through John Deere Financial give it one of the strongest sales and service channels in farm equipment.

longterm.evidence: Deere kept R&D rising to $1.704B in the first nine months of FY2026 (from $1.631B) despite a farm downturn, prioritising technology over short-term profit.

gr1.evidence: FY2025 net sales and revenues were $45.7B, with a market value of about $174B.

ni10.evidence: Deere was profitable in every year from FY2016 to FY2025, with net income between $2.75B (FY2020) and $10.17B (FY2023) over FY2019-FY2025.

gr4.evidence: Deere has paid dividends every year for decades, with dividends declared rising from $1.52 a share in FY2011 to $6.33 paid in FY2025.

eps10.evidence: Diluted EPS rose from $5.77 in FY2015 to $18.50 in FY2025, more than tripling.

gr6.evidence: The price is about 24 times average FY2023-FY2025 EPS of $26.25.

gr7.evidence: P/E of about 36 times P/B of about 6.2 gives roughly 220, far above 22.5.

th1.evidence: Deere's precision tech leads but is not ten times better than CNH, AGCO/PTx Trimble or CLAAS offerings.

timing.evidence: Autonomy and computer vision are maturing and labor is scarce, but FY2026 US and Canada large-ag demand is still guided down 15-20%.

th3.evidence: Deere began as a plow maker in 1837 and grew in a broad market, not from dominating a small niche.

team.evidence: Management under John May is strong and disciplined but not an exceptional founder-led team.

th5.evidence: Its dealer network plus John Deere Financial give it a powerful way to reach, sell to and finance customers.

durable.evidence: A 189-year history, the largest installed base and over 520 million engaged acres in its Operations Center make its position likely to hold for decades.

th7.evidence: Precision agriculture and autonomy are widely recognised opportunities pursued by all major rivals.

trend.evidence: Deere benefits from farm automation and AI-based computer vision, and its construction business from data-center and infrastructure building, but it is not a leading AI beneficiary.

dr1.evidence: Q3 FY2026 EPS of $5.10 beat the $4.79 Zacks consensus and Deere raised its FY2026 net income outlook to $4.75-5.00B from $4.00-4.75B, though full-year earnings are still below FY2025's $5.03B.

dr2.evidence: Large-ag replacement demand and low used-tractor inventories (down nearly 40% year on year) point to recovery, but tariff costs rise to about $1B a year in FY2027.

dr4.evidence: Lower interest rates would help farmers finance equipment and Deere's finance arm, but weak crop prices and tariffs work against it.

dr6.evidence: A large-ag cycle turn, construction backlogs extending into FY2027 and tariff refunds ($382M recognised year to date in FY2026) could lift results.

dr7.evidence: High quality supports a sizeable position, but the high cyclical multiple limits conviction for a concentrated bet.

gm.evidence: Equipment gross margin was about 27.6% in FY2025, solid for industrial machinery but not high.

fcfyield.evidence: FY2025 free cash flow of about $6.1B is roughly a 3.5% yield on a $174B market value, modest for a cyclical.

gb2.evidence: FY2025 operating profit of $6.0B is under 3% of an enterprise value of roughly $227B.

pa2.evidence: The current weakness comes from a cyclical farm downturn and tariffs, both of which are temporary rather than structural.

pa4.evidence: Deere's market leadership, positive equity of $27.99B and essential products make permanent loss of the business unlikely, though price risk remains.

wo1.evidence: Deere is a leader in agricultural robotics and computer vision through Blue River Technology and autonomous tractors.

wo2.evidence: Its machines are not falling quickly in cost with volume; Deere still realizes positive price increases.

wo3.evidence: It combines robotics, AI computer vision, satellite connectivity and data software in its tech stack.

wo4.evidence: Deere's own 2030 ambition is a 10% annual sales growth rate, not a many-fold expansion of its market.

ac3.evidence: Demand depends on crop prices, farm incomes, interest rates, housing and tariffs.

ns1.evidence: Deere shares value through input savings (over 50% herbicide savings reported with See & Spray) but keeps raising prices rather than passing on scale savings.

ns4.evidence: Growing tech adoption and data lock-in could strengthen Deere, but right-to-repair rules and rival tech may offset some gains.

va2.evidence: It addresses labor shortages, input costs and the need to grow more food on the same land.

tn1.evidence: Deere sells into automation and infrastructure trends, but it is an old machinery company retrofitting technology rather than one built for the trend.

tn2.evidence: The market often sees Deere as a tractor maker, while it is building a software and autonomy platform with over 520 million engaged acres.

tn3.evidence: Deere is a large US company, not Chinese or a startup, but its sales are seasonal and tied to commodity cycles.

tn4.evidence: It is profitable, but revenue fell in FY2024 and FY2025 and debt of $63.8B exceeds cash of $10.3B, though most debt funds the finance arm.

tn5.evidence: Consolidated debt of $63.8B has far exceeded cash in every recent quarter.

tn6.evidence: Revenue fell 11.7% in FY2025 and analysts expect about 5.7% equipment sales growth in FY2026.

tn7.evidence: Revenue growth of about -12% in FY2025 plus a free-cash-flow margin of about 13% is far below 40.

tn8.evidence: In Q3 FY2026 revenue rose 5% while net income rose 7%, but over FY2025 revenue fell faster than costs as margins shrank.

tn9.evidence: Debt exceeds cash, operating margin is about 13% and revenue growth is below 10%.

tn10.evidence: The FTC right-to-repair case was settled in July 2026 with 10 years of obligations, and a $99M repair class-action was settled, but tariffs remain a major policy risk.

tn11.evidence: Deere provides farm and construction machines and precision tech that help farmers and builders do more work with less labor and inputs, and charges through equipment sales, parts, subscriptions and financing.

tn13.evidence: Approximate total 70: cash vs debt 0, revenue growth 0, operating margin 5, short interest 10, institutional ownership 10, revenue faster than expenses 5, 5-year return vs S&P 0, moat 10, CEO 5, pricing power 10, secular trend 5, culture 5, talent 5.

tn14.evidence: Revenue fell in FY2024 and FY2025, margins fell from the FY2023 peak, and debt exceeded cash every year.

tn15.evidence: Consolidated operating profit of $6.02B covered $3.17B of interest only about 1.9 times (equipment operations alone about 13 times), and assets excluding goodwill were only about 1.27 times liabilities.

tn18.evidence: John May has led since 2019 with strong execution, including record FY2023 profit, but has under 10 years in the role, is not the founder, and no notable open-market buying is known.

tn20.evidence: Deere beat the Q3 FY2026 consensus ($5.10 vs $4.79), but a full multi-quarter surprise record was not verified.

tn21.evidence: There is no clown CEO, co-CEO, fraud or auditor change, but margins declined from FY2023 to FY2025.

tn22.evidence: Deere has $45.7B of revenue, steady profits and a falling share count, the opposite of a hype stock.

tn24.evidence: At about 36 times trough earnings the price implies a strong recovery and growth well above Deere's recent revenue decline.

tn25.evidence: With negative three-year average revenue growth and about $6.1B of free cash flow, a 12% DCF minus about $53.6B of net debt gives a value far below $641.63 a share.

tn26.evidence: The P/E of about 36 is high versus machinery peers and modest near-term EPS growth gives a PEG well above 1.
